title: Norm Anchors Make Model Edits Last
claim: Existing increment-level controls leave the norm-feedback loop unresolved so weights grow; anchoring the solved value bounds norms and keeps edits stable.
layout: 3 zones, left-to-right; optimizer box feeds red-versus-blue branching outcome panels
description: The figure reads left to right. On the left, a gray grid labeled W_{n-1} (edited weights) feeds into a rounded box titled OPTIMIZER, which lists three existing increment-level controls: value-norm regularization (penalize ||Δv||), matrix-norm regularization (penalize ||ΔW||_F) and a value-update clamp (clip Δv). Each control has a small icon. A red arrow labeled 'Unanchored solved value' v_n^new splits into two branches. The top red panel, 'X NO NAS PLUGIN', shows larger ||ΔW_n||_F leading to a red grid of larger W_n and rising bars, with a robot mascot holding scissors saying 'breaks norm-feedback'. The bottom blue panel, '✓ WITH NAS PLUGIN', shows the NAS Anchor box (anchor icon, original-model norm τ, formula v_n = τ v̂_n/||v̂_n||). It leads to a stable ||ΔW_n||_F, a blue grid of stable W_n and bounded bars. Red versus blue contrast draws the eye first.
caption: Mechanism illustration. NAS anchors the solved value before writing, breaking the norm-feedback loop left unresolved by increment-level controls.
abstract: Sequential Locate-and-Edit (L&E) model editing can fail abruptly after many edits. We identify and formalize this failure as a positive norm-feedback loop, in which solved value vectors and edited MLP weights progressively amplify each other, degrading edit quality and eventually collapsing model capabilities. Our analysis shows that this feedback can yield approximately exponential norm growth under standard L&E dynamics, and can remain unresolved by existing increment-level regularizers or update clamps. We propose Norm-Anchor Scaling (NAS), a plug-in stabilizer that breaks this loop by rescaling each solved value vector to an original-model reference norm. Across multiple LLM backbones, datasets, and L&E editors, NAS extends the usable editing horizon by more than 4x and improves long-run editing performance by 72.2% on average, while preserving single-edit efficacy, with only a one-line modification and negligible computational overhead.
